--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
EMPIRICAL RESEARCH PLAN
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

1. Identification Strategy  
Method: Fuzzy Regression Discontinuity Design (RDD) combined with a 2-stage least-squares (RD-IV).

Why appropriate  
• Assignment to Russell 2000 vs. Russell 1000 changes sharply at the rank = 1,000 cutoff each June.  
• Firms just above/below the cutoff are virtually identical ex-ante, so local differences can be attributed to the shock.  
• Membership is not perfectly deterministic (banding rules, free-float adjustments), so the first-stage jump in liquidity is less than one; hence a fuzzy RD.  
• The discontinuity supplies a powerful instrument for liquidity, allowing us to estimate the causal effect of liquidity on innovation (second stage).

2. Treatment and Control  

Treatment variable  
Treated = 1 if the firm is assigned to (and actually enters) the Russell 2000 in year t; 0 if it enters the Russell 1000.

Control group  
Firms ranked just above the cutoff (950 – 1,050 bandwidth to start) that enter the Russell 1000 serve as the counterfactual.

Running variable  
r_it = the firm’s rank by float-adjusted market capitalization on the annual rank list used by FTSE Russell.

Cutoff  
c = 1,000.  

Treatment timing  
Event date τ is the final trading day in June of each year (reconstitution date). Outcomes are measured in fiscal years t, t+1, … relative to τ (e.g., patents granted in the next three calendar years).

3. Key Identifying Assumptions  

A1. Local continuity of potential outcomes: Expected innovation and liquidity would evolve smoothly in rank absent the index switch.  
Plausibility: Firms around the boundary are observationally similar; no mechanical change in fundamentals at exactly rank = 1,000.

A2. No precise manipulation of the running variable: Firms cannot fine-tune their float-adjusted market cap on the reference date with the precision needed to select index status.  
Plausibility: Float shares and prices are largely market-driven; past tests (e.g., Chang, Hong & Liskovich 2015) show no bunching.

A3. First-stage relevance: Russell membership causes a discrete jump in liquidity (bid-ask spread ↓, turnover ↑).  
Plausibility: Extensively documented in the index‐inclusion literature.

A4. Exclusion restriction for RD-IV: Membership affects innovation only through the change in liquidity, not through other mechanisms that also jump at the cutoff.  
Plausibility: Main alternative channel is change in institutional ownership; we will control/verify.

A5. Stable Unit Treatment Value (SUTVA): One firm’s index status/liquidity does not directly change another boundary firm’s innovation.  
Plausibility: Reasonable in this setting.

4. Main Threats & Mitigations  

T1. Strategic window-dressing of market cap (violates A2).  
   – McCrary density test of ranks; placebo RD on pre-ranking price run-ups.  
   – Drop firms involved in large equity issues or buybacks ±60 days around the rank date.

T2. Other mechanisms jump at the cutoff (violates A4).  
   – Document discontinuities in analyst coverage, institutional ownership, CEO incentives, etc.  
   – Include those covariates in the second stage; show results robust to controlling for them.  
   – Perform a “donut” RD excluding the ±5 ranks around 1,000 to alleviate simultaneous treatments.

T3. Anticipation or lag in innovation outcomes.  
   – Use pre-trend checks: RD on patent counts in t-1, t-2. Expect no jump.  
   – Estimate dynamic effects (event-time dummies τ +1 … τ +5) to verify timing.

5. R Code Outline  

```r
# Load packages
library(data.table)
library(fixest)     # fast fe and iv regressions
library(rdrobust)   # RD estimation
library(ggplot2)

# 1. Data load -------------------------------------------------------------
ri  <- fread("russell_memberships_1990_2006.csv")   # firm-year, rank, R1000/2000 dummy
liq <- fread("taq_microstructure.csv")              # firm-day liquidity measures
pat <- fread("nber_patents.csv")                    # patents granted & citations
cmp <- fread("compustat_fundamentals.csv")

# 2. Merge & variable construction ----------------------------------------
df <- merge(ri, cmp,  by = c("permno","year"))
df <- merge(df, liq,  by = c("permno","year"))
df <- merge(df, pat,  by = c("permno","year"), all.x = TRUE)

# Running variable and treatment
df[, running := rank]                    # rank (ascending)
df[, treat   := as.integer(r2000 == 1)]  # actual inclusion

# Liquidity proxy: annual avg bid‐ask %
df[, spread_pa := mean_pct_spread]

# Innovation outcomes (forward 3-yr sums)
setorder(df, permno, year)
df[, patents_f3 := shift(patents, 1, type="lead") +
                      shift(patents, 2, type="lead") +
                      shift(patents, 3, type="lead"),
   by = permno]

# Subset to symmetric initial bandwidth
bw0 <- 100              # ranks 900–1100
sample <- df[running >= (1000 - bw0) & running <= (1000 + bw0)]

# 3. First-stage: does membership increase liquidity? ----------------------
fs <- rdrobust(y = sample$spread_pa, x = sample$running,
               c = 1000, fuzzy = sample$treat)
summary(fs)

# 4. Second stage (RD-IV within fixest) ------------------------------------
# Local polynomial order 1, triangular weights
sample[, w := (1 - abs(running - 1000)/bw0)]  # linear triangular weight
model_iv <- feols(patents_f3 ~ 1 | 0 | 
                 (liq_proxy = treat), 
                 data = sample,
                 weights = ~w,
                 subset = abs(running - 1000) <= bw0)

summary(model_iv)

# 5. Robustness: vary bandwidth & placebo cutoffs --------------------------
bw_vec <- c(50, 75, 125, 150)
ro <- lapply(bw_vec, function(bw) {
  feols(patents_f3 ~ 1 | 0 | (liq_proxy = treat),
        data = sample,
        subset = abs(running - 1000) <= bw,
        weights = ~ (1 - abs(running - 1000)/bw))
})
etable(ro, se = "ser")

# Placebo cutoff at 900
placebo <- feols(patents_f3 ~ 1 | 0 | (liq_proxy = treat),
                 data = df[abs(rank - 900) <= 100])
summary(placebo)
```

6. Expected Results  

Prior: Higher liquidity (smaller spreads, larger turnover) shortens investors’ horizons and intensifies monitoring pressure, potentially discouraging long-term R&D that yields uncertain payoffs. Hence the local‐average treatment effect is expected to be negative. Magnitude: a 1 ppt drop in bid-ask spread (or one-sd rise in turnover) is expected to reduce the 3-year forward patent count by roughly 5 – 10 %. Citations likely fall by a similar or slightly larger proportion.

7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (RDD)  
C1. Large discrete jump in treatment at the cutoff …… 1  
C2. No manipulation of running variable …………………… 0.8 (minor concern)  
C3. Covariate balance across cutoff ………………………… 1  
C4. Correct functional form / bandwidth robustness …… 1  
C5. No other discontinuous shocks at cutoff ……………… 0.6 (some concern)  

Total (out of 5) = 4.4 → “reasonably credible”.
